rationale: Verifying a secret against a stored credential is user authentication, with no statement about what data is protected from disclosure.
Sensitive data must not be exposed to third parties without owner permission, which is a confidentiality requirement.
Restricts visibility of link topology information to authorised roles only.
A valid authentication code with a session key detects alteration and verifies the origin of the top-up instruction.
Detecting resubmitted one-time codes and treating them as replay attempts is replay-attack resistance.
Biometric fingerprint matching identifies residents before granting access.
Restricts who can change write privileges and uses digests to identify tampering with loaded data.
Keys are kept in a tamper-resistant module so key material is never readable outside it, protecting against disclosure.
Face matching against enrolled templates identifies residents before unlocking.
Limits who may modify or cancel a reservation, an integrity access restriction.
Two-factor verification of customer identity before payment is authentication.
Only ETL jobs and administrators with write privileges may modify tables, restricting modification.
Encrypts exchanged data and withholds it from devices that have not proven their identity, covering confidentiality and device authentication.
An HMAC check flags audit files whose content no longer matches, detecting alteration.
Prevents modules from disabling malicious-activity detection and blocking, preserving attack resistance.
Public-key encryption protects pairing secrets from disclosure to eavesdroppers.
Releases medical history only to assigned clinicians, restricting read access.
Wiping a guest's collected occupancy and routine data is a privacy requirement.
Bit-for-bit comparison with the published package verifies the extension has not been altered.
Detecting and rejecting files crafted to trigger buffer overflows is resistance to attack.
Stored data may only be read by issuer-approved readers, which restricts reading and implies reader authentication.
Blocking all requests from an extension revoked as malicious, persistently, contains a malicious component.
A digital signature makes alteration of the discharge summary detectable.
The purpose of detecting duplicate provenance marks is not stated, so whether it concerns origin or alteration cannot be decided.
Blocking clients that exceed a request rate limits abuse such as flooding.
Aborting prescriptions whose fields mismatch a protected checksum detects data alteration.
Validating format and consistency of entries before saving is data validity checking.
Verifying the PIN against the stored value before unlocking is authentication.
Checking configuration against signed reference values and restoring differences protects data from unauthorised modification.
Confirming account ownership through the registered email is identity verification.
Ensures extensions cannot disable or evade intrusion-detection and throttling controls.
Demanding an anti-automation challenge after repeated rejected requests counters bot flooding.
A decoy server to detect and block intruders is attack detection and defence.
Unauthorised terminals are refused any command that would change the stored balance, restricting modification.
Requires identification by account and matching credential before connecting.
Validating the server certificate chain and expiry authenticates the server before data exchange.
Signature verification of extensions detects tampering and checks origin before running.
Behavioural biometric matching establishes developer identity.
Credential check verifies customer identity before granting session access.
